title: 03 — Memory Management
html:
03 — Memory Management

The one idea: peak memory is decided by two choices: how many bytes each value takes (its type), and how much of the data is materialised at once (eager vs streaming). Get both right and a laptop handles data many times its RAM.

1. What it is

Lever Effect
Smaller types (Int16 instead of Int64, Float32 where precision allows) Fewer bytes per value
Enum for a fixed, known set of labels One small integer per row plus one dictionary
Categorical for labels discovered at run time Integer codes plus a dictionary, larger codes than Enum here
Lazy scan_* with pushdown Only needed rows and columns are ever loaded
Streaming engine (the lazy default in Polars 2) Data flows through in batches, so peak memory stays near one batch per thread
sink_* The result goes straight to a file, never fully in memory
collect_batches Results arrive in chunks for a consumer
Spilling to disk (out-of-core) When a memory budget is hit, operations such as sort spill to a temp directory

2. Why it matters

  • An out-of-memory kill is the most common way a data job fails on a laptop, a container or a small VM.
  • Containers are killed at their memory limit with no warning, often long before the host runs out.
  • Smaller data is also faster: less to read, scan and move between cores.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Measure before you guess

  • df.estimated_size("mb") gives the in-memory size of a frame or column.
  • pl.read_parquet_schema(path) and scan_parquet(path).collect_schema() give types without reading data.
  • Peak memory of a whole process: resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss (KB on Linux), measured in a fresh process per experiment.

3.2 Type choices

Data Prefer
Small integer ranges Int8/Int16/Int32 (Series.shrink_dtype() finds the smallest. Expr.shrink_dtype was removed in 2.0)
Money Decimal(p, s), or integers in the smallest unit (paise, cents)
Fixed label sets (side, status, category) Enum([...]). It also rejects unknown values
Dates without time Date, not Datetime or strings
Long repeated text Categorical, or keep String. Measure, because it is not always smaller

3.3 Eager vs lazy, measured

Eager read_parquet loads every column of every row, then computes. A lazy scan with the streaming engine reads only what the plan needs, a batch at a time.

3.4 Spilling to disk (out-of-core)

The Polars 2 streaming engine can spill to disk when memory runs short. The Polars 2.1 binary reads environment variables for this, such as POLARS_OOC_MEMORY_BUDGET_MB and POLARS_TEMP_DIR. These are not documented in the user guide yet, so treat them as unstable, and pin the Polars version if you rely on them. Point the temp directory at a fast local disk with space to spare.

---
title: How memory stays bounded in a streaming query
---
flowchart LR
    F["Parquet files"] -- "only needed<br/>columns and row groups" --> S["Scan (batches)"]
    S --> P["Filter / project / aggregate<br/>per batch, all cores"]
    P -- "over budget" --> D["Spill to temp dir"]
    D --> P
    P --> K["sink_parquet<br/>(written as it goes)"]

4. Working code

4.1 Column sizes and peak memory

The script compares column sizes by type, then answers one question (total amount per account over 30 million rows) three ways, each in a fresh process.

import os, subprocess, sys
import polars as pl

# 1. What a column costs: pick the smallest type that holds the data.
n = 1_000_000
codes = ["EQUITY", "DEBT", "HYBRID", "INDEX", "LIQUID"]
df = pl.DataFrame({
    "qty_i64": pl.int_range(n, eager=True) % 1_000,
    "category": pl.Series([codes[i % 5] for i in range(n)]),
})
df = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("qty_i64").cast(pl.Int16).alias("qty_i16"),
    pl.col("category").cast(pl.Categorical).alias("category_cat"),
    pl.col("category").cast(pl.Enum(codes)).alias("category_enum"),
)
for name in df.columns:
    print(f"{name:<14} {df[name].dtype.base_type()!s:<12} {df[name].estimated_size('mb'):6.2f} MB")
# Polars 2 removed Expr.shrink_dtype; the Series method remains.
print("Series.shrink_dtype picks:", df["qty_i64"].shrink_dtype().dtype)

# 2. Peak memory of three ways to answer the same question, each in a fresh process.
os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
if not os.path.exists("data/big.parquet"):
    rows = 30_000_000
    (pl.LazyFrame({"id": pl.int_range(rows, eager=True)})
       .with_columns((pl.col("id") % 5_000).alias("account"),
                     ((pl.col("id") * 7919) % 100_000 / 100).alias("amount"),
                     pl.format("txn-{}", pl.col("id")).alias("ref"))
       .sink_parquet("data/big.parquet"))
print("\ninput:", round(os.path.getsize("data/big.parquet") / 1e6), "MB parquet, 30,000,000 rows")

runner = r'''
import resource, sys, polars as pl
mode = sys.argv[1]
if mode == "eager read_parquet":
    df = pl.read_parquet("data/big.parquet")
    out = df.group_by("account").agg(pl.col("amount").sum())
elif mode == "lazy scan, collect":
    out = (pl.scan_parquet("data/big.parquet")
           .group_by("account").agg(pl.col("amount").sum()).collect())
elif mode == "lazy scan, sink to file":
    (pl.scan_parquet("data/big.parquet").filter(pl.col("amount") > 900)
       .sink_parquet("data/filtered.parquet"))
    out = pl.scan_parquet("data/filtered.parquet").select(pl.len()).collect()
peak_mb = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss / 1024
print(f"{mode:<26} peak {peak_mb:7.0f} MB   result rows {out.height}")
'''
for mode in ["eager read_parquet", "lazy scan, collect", "lazy scan, sink to file"]:
    print(subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", runner, mode], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())

Output:

qty_i64        Int64          7.63 MB
category       String         5.15 MB
qty_i16        Int16          1.91 MB
category_cat   Categorical    3.81 MB
category_enum  Enum           0.95 MB
Series.shrink_dtype picks: Int16

input: 91 MB parquet, 30,000,000 rows
eager read_parquet         peak    2645 MB   result rows 5000
lazy scan, collect         peak     527 MB   result rows 5000
lazy scan, sink to file    peak     527 MB   result rows 1

What to notice:

  • Int16 is a quarter of Int64, and Enum is a fifth of String for five labels. Categorical was 4× larger than Enum here, because its codes are wider.
  • Eager reading peaked at about 2.6 GB, lazy scanning at about 530 MB, five times less for the same answer. The 91 MB file grows about 20× once decompressed into memory, which is why "it's only a 91 MB file" is a trap.
  • Sinking a filtered result to a file stayed at the same low peak. The result never had to fit in memory.

4.2 Spilling a large sort to disk

import os, subprocess, sys

# Sort 30 million rows by a text column, streaming the result to a file, in a fresh process each time.
# The POLARS_OOC_* settings exist in Polars 2.1 but are not documented yet: treat them as unstable.
probe = """
import resource, polars as pl
pl.scan_parquet("data/big.parquet").sort("ref").sink_parquet("data/sorted.parquet")
print(round(resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss / 1024))
"""
os.makedirs("data/spill", exist_ok=True)
for label, extra in [
    ("no budget", {}),
    ("300 MB budget", {"POLARS_OOC_MEMORY_BUDGET_MB": "300", "POLARS_TEMP_DIR": os.path.abspath("data/spill")}),
]:
    peak = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", probe], env={**os.environ, **extra},
                          capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
    print(f"sort 30M rows, {label:<14} peak {peak} MB")

Output:

sort 30M rows, no budget      peak 2172 MB
sort 30M rows, 300 MB budget  peak 414 MB

What to notice:

  • A 300 MB budget cut the peak from about 2.2 GB to about 410 MB. In earlier runs on this machine, it took about 3× longer (3 s to 9 s) because sorted runs were written to and read back from disk.
  • Use it when the alternative is an out-of-memory kill. When memory allows, the in-memory run is faster.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Judging memory by file size. Compressed Parquet can expand 10–30× in memory.
  2. read_* on large files when only a few columns or rows are needed.
  3. Int64 and String everywhere because that is what inference produced.
  4. Collecting a large result just to write it, instead of sink_parquet.
  5. Assuming Categorical is always smaller. Measure it, and prefer Enum for known sets.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Add pl.col("ref").cast(pl.Categorical) to the 30-million-row query and measure peak memory and time.
  2. Run the eager version inside a container with a 1 GB memory limit (docker run -m 1g ...) and watch it get killed. Then run the lazy version.
  3. Try budgets of 200, 500 and 1,000 MB for the sort and plot peak memory against time.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. How do you find a frame's in-memory size?
  2. Why is Enum smaller and safer than String for a status column?
  3. Why did the lazy query use far less memory than the eager one?
  4. When should you use sink_parquet instead of collect()?
  5. What is the trade-off of spilling to disk?

Answers

  1. df.estimated_size("mb"), or per column with df[col].estimated_size().
  2. Each row stores a small integer code, and values outside the declared set are rejected.
  3. Projection and predicate pushdown read only the needed data, and the streaming engine processes it in batches.
  4. When the result is going to a file anyway, or is too large to hold in memory.
  5. Bounded memory in exchange for extra disk I/O and a slower run.
